claims.claim: A large language model (LLM) is a deep learning model trained on immense amounts of data that is capable of understanding and generating natural language and other types of content, built on a transformer neural network architecture.

LLMs work as statistical prediction machines that repeatedly predict the next word in a sequence; they learn patterns in text during training and generate language that follows those patterns. Text is broken into tokens (words, subwords, or characters) that the model reads and generates one at a time.

LLM training starts with a massive amount of data — billions or trillions of words from books, articles, websites, code, and other text sources; the transformer architecture (introduced in 2017) made training at this scale practical, and trained models can hold billions or trillions of parameters. Scale of training data is the defining feature of the approach.

As of the sources read in August 2026, LLMs handle tasks including summarizing an article, debugging code, drafting a legal clause, translation and multilingual capabilities, and explaining complex concepts in simpler terms; OpenAI's documentation states models can generate almost any kind of text response — code, mathematical equations, structured data, or human-like prose.

LLMs can generate information that is false or misleading while sounding plausible (hallucinations, which IBM lists among major accuracy concerns), and NIST's Generative AI Profile documents confabulation — 'the production of confidently stated but erroneous or false content' — as a risk by which users may be misled or deceived. Fluency is not accuracy.

Large language models are the text-focused family of generative AI — as of IBM's 2026 description, the most common foundation models, created for text-generation applications — within the broader generative AI family that also covers image, video, and sound models.

LLMs can reflect and amplify biases present in their training data, producing outputs that are unfair or offensive, and their training and operation require large amounts of computational power and energy.

Because confabulation is documented, users should verify important LLM output — facts, citations, and numbers — against reliable sources before acting on it; NIST's Generative AI Profile frames provenance tracking and verification as part of managing generative AI risk.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether LLM output can be described as 'understanding' language
positions: IBM's explainer says LLMs are 'capable of understanding and generating natural language'
The same source describes the mechanism as statistical prediction of the next word, with no claim that the model possesses human-like comprehension or checks facts
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson uses 'understand and generate' when describing the model's behavior in IBM's terms, but explains the mechanism as pattern prediction and explicitly avoids claiming the model comprehends meaning, checks facts, or has awareness.

conflictingEvidence.issue: How strongly to state current LLM capabilities
positions: Provider documentation (IBM, OpenAI) describes summarizing, drafting, translating, explaining, and code assistance as current capabilities
Specific tools, model versions, and quality change quickly, and capabilities vary by model and task
conflictingEvidence.resolution: All capability claims are time-anchored ('as of the sources read in August 2026') and phrased as general capabilities documented by the providers, never as timeless facts; the lesson notes that specific tools and quality keep changing.

sourceRecords.title: What are large language models (LLMs)?
sourceRecords.notes: Read live via curl with a browser user-agent on 2026-08-21. Primary source for the lesson's core claims: LLMs as deep learning models trained on immense amounts of data, capable of understanding and generating natural language; LLMs as statistical prediction machines that repeatedly predict the next word in a sequence; training starting with billions or trillions of words from books, articles, websites, code, and other text sources; tokenization into words, subwords, or characters; the transformer architecture introduced in 2017; parameters numbering in the billions or trillions; capabilities including summarizing an article, debugging code, drafting a legal clause, translation and multilingual capabilities, and explaining complex concepts in simpler terms; hallucinations as false or misleading output that sounds plausible; bias amplification and resource demands as limitations; LLMs as the most common foundation models for text generation; and popular interfaces including Claude, ChatGPT, Copilot, Llama, and Gemini. Facts paraphrased into original prose; no wording reproduced.
